note: The turning year in Harr, on the host computer's calendar. Four seasons, each with a short blurb for the three weekly rhythms of the village (ids match content/veloren-events.json) and twelve extra field notes for the library, spread over the ten discovery places (ids match content/veloren-discoveries.json). Everything here is scripted, peaceful and additive: it never replaces the base notes or blurbs.

events.blurb: Seedlings in little clay pots, early greens and bundles of herbs are laid out. Take a pot home and watch it wake up.
Scholars read the first field notes of the year, and everyone adds what they saw come back to life.
The spring festival: round dances on the plaza under blossom, and a long table of everything the fields have started.

notes.text: The yellow clover band is first to open in spring, and the earliest bees arrive within a day of the first petals.
Counting flowers in a one-metre square each week shows the bands thickening from three kinds in early March to seven by May.
Meltwater darkens the stone's southern face each spring while the north face stays dry, so the lichen colours are easiest to compare now.
Spring rain raises the pool by a hand's width, yet the water stays clear and cold, so the filtering gravel evidently works at any flow.
From the high view, new green spreads up the valley from the river side first, and a scholar can mark the date it reaches each field.
On the first warm morning the colony sends out scouts in large numbers, and the hollow hums noticeably louder by mid-April.
Lichen swells and brightens after spring showers, which is the best week to measure the edge of each patch against the marked stone.
Spring is when the dawn chorus fills out: chaffinch, blackbird and wren return and the scholars' score gains new lines each week.
The bank is soft and easy to work after spring rain, so makers take what they need early and smooth the cut before it dries.
Spring nights bring the galaxy season: with the meadow dark, the long band of the Milky Way can be seen climbing after midnight.
Steady spring winds make this the best season to log wind speed for the mill plans kept in the library.
Frogspawn appears in the quiet corner of the spring pool in March, and small tadpoles can be counted from the stepping stones by April.

events.blurb: Berries, cucumbers, lemon balm tea and sun-hats on the stalls. The market hall's shade is the best seat in Harr.
Long evenings: scholars read aloud in the late light while the fireflies of the field pavilion begin to glow.
The midsummer festival: lanterns strung across the plaza, picnic blankets everywhere, and music until the stars come out.

notes.text: At midsummer all seven flower kinds bloom together, and the bands of colour are clearest from the top of the meadow in the morning.
The stone holds the day's warmth long after sunset, which shows that rock this dense stores heat the way a hearth does.
On the hottest afternoons the pool remains cold to the touch, a living reminder that the spring draws from deep underground.
Summer haze softens the far ridges, but at dawn the whole valley is crisp, and the best day for a map-making walk is the first clear morning after rain.
At the height of summer, fanning bees line up at the hollow entrance to cool the hive, a good lesson in cooperation to watch quietly.
In dry summer weeks the lichen shrinks and turns pale grey, then recovers fully within an hour of the next shower.
By summer the chorus is quieter after dawn, but young birds practise their songs in the grove all afternoon.
Dry summer clay is easy to carry home in lumps, and makers who dried it on the bank's sunny shelf report it keeps its colour well.
August brings the meteor showers; lying on the meadow grass with a notebook, a scholar can count a shooting star every few minutes.
Afternoon breezes on the ridge rise reliably by two o'clock in summer, a pattern the library's mill plans now rely on.
Butterflies visit the purple vetch from midday; four kinds have been drawn into the meadow notebook so far.
Swifts scream high above the grove on summer evenings, chasing insects that rise on the warm air.

events.blurb: Apples, squash, jars of jam and bundles of dried herbs. Farmers swap seeds for next year with anyone who asks.
Scholars read the harvest notes: what grew, what taught us something, and what we will try differently next year.
The harvest festival: a long shared table of everything the fields gave, with thanks said to every hand that helped.

notes.text: Seed heads ripen in autumn; collecting a few from each of the seven kinds for the heirloom seed shelf keeps the meadow's bands going.
Fallen leaves gather against the stone's lee side, and the moss beneath keeps the base damp and green long into November.
Autumn leaves drift across the pool and settle in the gravel, and the water stays just as clear, a good sign of a healthy spring.
From the high view autumn paints the valley in bands of amber and copper, and the winding road shows clearly between the colours.
In autumn the colony gathers its last pollen and the hollow smells of honey; the keepers take only a small share and leave plenty for winter.
Autumn mist feeds the lichen directly, and the patches visibly plump up; it is the best season to photograph their colours.
Autumn brings migrants through the grove for a few days at a time, and scholars add their names to the visitors' list.
Autumn is when makers fire their pots in the kilns, and the bank's red clay turns the warm terracotta that matches the leaves.
Clear autumn nights are long and crisp, ideal for charting the great square of Pegasus rising above the eastern trees.
Autumn winds are gustier on the ridge, which gives the mill planners useful data on how the sails should handle changing speeds.
Late asters keep the meadow in colour well into October, and the last bees of the year feed on them in the midday sun.
Leaf prints pressed into damp clay make lovely tiles, and the makers' autumn workshop has filled a whole shelf with them.

events.blurb: Warm bread, root vegetables from the cellar, knitted scarves and mugs of hot tea. The stalls glow with lamps from early afternoon.
Scholars and keepers read by lamplight in the pavilion, and the oldest tales of the valley are told while tea is passed round.
The winter festival: a ring of lanterns on the plaza, hot cider, and a promise said together that the light will come back.

notes.text: Under frost the meadow looks asleep, but the rosettes of leaves visible near the ground show that every kind is waiting for spring.
Frost lines etch the stone's surface into delicate patterns, and the north face stays white long after the sun has warmed the south.
On the coldest mornings the spring pool steams softly while the rest of the valley is frozen, because its water stays at seven degrees all year.
In winter the bare trees open long sightlines, and from the high view every future cottage plot can be seen at once.
In winter the colony clusters tightly inside the hollow and keeps warm by taking turns at the cold outer edge; the keepers listen at the bark, never disturbing them.
Lichen keeps growing slowly through winter whenever the day is damp and above freezing, so the measuring stakes are checked even in January.
Robins and wrens sing through winter mornings, and the quiet grove is the easiest place to learn each voice one at a time.
Frost splits the exposed clay face into neat flakes, and makers wait until spring to dig so that the bank can rest.
Winter has the longest, darkest nights, and Orion stands bright over the meadow, an easy first constellation for new scholars.
Steady winter winds make the ridge the best place for the village's wind readings, kept in the library for the mill plans.
Fresh snow shows the tracks of small visitors in the grove, and the scholars sketch each print without disturbing a thing.
Even when ice rims the pool, the water in the middle keeps flowing, and the well downstream stays full all winter.

chronicle.note: Twenty milestone phrases the chronicle can use; {project} is a project's name. Then one finishing line for each of the 36 public works, keyed by project id.

milestones.ground-broken: Ground was marked out for {project}, and the first neighbours came to help.
milestones.first-stage: The first stage of {project} is up, built by a crew standing together.
milestones.second-stage: {project} gained its second stage, and the plan took shape.
milestones.halfway: {project} is halfway built, and the neighbours stopped to admire it.
milestones.last-stage-near: Only one stage remains of {project}, and a crew is already gathering.
milestones.finished: {project} was finished, and the whole village came to see.
milestones.first-visit: The first visitors walked through {project} and said it felt like home.
milestones.opening-day: {project} was opened with a shared meal and a quiet round of thanks.
milestones.crew-of-two: Two neighbours stood together at {project}, and the next stage began.
milestones.crew-of-many: A large crew gathered at {project}, and the work went by like a song.
milestones.first-find: A new page was written for the library, the first of many.
milestones.fifth-find: Five places are now in the library, and the valley feels a little smaller.
milestones.tenth-find: The catalogue is complete: all ten places are written down for all to read.
milestones.first-meal: The first meal was shared from the pantry, and the farmers smiled.
milestones.hundredth-meal: A hundred portions have been shared at the pantry table.
milestones.market-held: Market hour was held on the plaza, and everyone found something to take home.
milestones.circle-held: Story circle was held, and a new page was added to what the village knows.
milestones.festival-held: The weekly festival filled the plaza with lamps, music and neighbours.
milestones.tech-learned: The village learned something new, and the research tower recorded it.
milestones.season-turned: The season turned, and the village wrote its new field notes.

projects.lantern-path: The lantern path was finished, and no one in Harr walks home in the dark.
projects.cottage-2: Cottage 2 was finished, with a bright window and a full woodpile from its builders.
projects.field-pavilion: The field pavilion was finished, and the first shared meal was eaten in its shade.
projects.library-annex: The library annex was finished, and the new shelves were filled by evening.
projects.cottage-3: Cottage 3 was finished, completing the first row of homes beside the plaza.
projects.orchard-gate: The orchard fence and gate were finished, and the young trees now grow in peace.
projects.research-tower: The research tower was finished, and the village's findings now stand in one bright view.

projects.light-fountain: The light fountain was finished, and neighbours rest beside it after a day's work.

projects.data-archive: The open archive was finished, and every finding in Harr is now kept for anyone to read.
projects.sky-walk: The sky walk was finished, and neighbours can see the whole village from above.
projects.glass-garden: The glass garden was finished, and flowers bloom there in every season.
projects.schoolhouse: The Harr schoolhouse was finished, and young and old sat down to learn together.
projects.seminar-pavilion: The seminar pavilion was finished, and the first talk was a happy crowd.
projects.workshop-hall: The makers' workshop hall was finished, and every bench was in use by noon.
projects.recycling-garden: The material recycling garden was finished, and nothing in Harr is wasted now.
projects.cottage-4: Cottage 4 was finished, with its skylights catching the first morning sun.
projects.cottage-5: Cottage 5 was finished, and a new family hung a lamp at the door.
projects.cottage-6: Cottage 6 was finished, and the third eco-cottage was ready for its neighbours.

captions.note: One sentence for each public work: what the building is for.

projects.well: The well gives the whole square fresh water, drawn from the hidden spring.
projects.market-hall: The market hall gives makers and farmers a roofed place to share what they have grown and made.
projects.cottage-1: Cottage 1 is a home for a newly arrived neighbour, raised by the village together.
projects.observatory: The observatory is a raised platform where scholars chart the night sky and write down what they learn.
projects.lantern-path: The lantern path lights the way from the plaza to the fields so that no one walks home in the dark.
projects.cottage-2: Cottage 2 is a home for a neighbour who has just arrived, built by many hands.
projects.field-pavilion: The field pavilion is a shaded place beside the fields for resting, reading and sharing meals.
projects.library-annex: The library annex gives the Harr Library more shelves, so that every discovery has a page.
projects.cottage-3: Cottage 3 is a home for newcomers, and it completes the first row beside the plaza.
projects.orchard-gate: The orchard gate lets everyone walk in to the trees while keeping the saplings safe as they grow.
projects.research-tower: The research tower gathers the village's findings into a single view for every scholar to read.
projects.solar-array: The solar array turns sunlight into the power that keeps the lamps and paths lit all night.
projects.vertical-farm: The vertical farm grows food in stacked, bright rooms so that more people can eat from less land.
projects.light-fountain: The light fountain is a quiet place to sit and rest at the end of a day of work.
projects.transit-hub: The transit hub is a platform for the quiet trains and landing pads that Harr hopes to have one day.
projects.data-archive: The open archive keeps every finding, plan and story where anyone, even a neighbouring village, can read it.
projects.sky-walk: The sky walk lifts neighbours above the square to cross it and to see the whole of Harr.
projects.glass-garden: The glass garden keeps plants and people warm in every season, with benches among the planters.
projects.schoolhouse: The schoolhouse is where young and old villagers learn reading, history and botany side by side.
projects.seminar-pavilion: The seminar pavilion is an open ring of columns where scholars talk ideas through and share their research.
projects.workshop-hall: The workshop hall is a roomy place where makers of cloth, wood and clay work at shared benches.
projects.recycling-garden: The recycling garden sorts spare clay, timber and metal so that it can be used again.
projects.cottage-4: Cottage 4 is an eco-cottage with solar skylights, a home for a neighbour who needs one.
projects.cottage-5: Cottage 5 is an eco-cottage that is bright and warm, a home for a Harr family.
projects.cottage-6: Cottage 6 is a split-level home with skylights, ready for a new resident of Harr.
projects.cottage-7: Cottage 7 is a sun-warmed dome home surrounded by planters of flowers.
projects.cottage-8: Cottage 8 is a dome home among flowering planters, built for a neighbour who is arriving.
projects.cottage-9: Cottage 9 is a stepped dome home that rounds out the ring of cottages around the planters.
projects.guesthouse: The guesthouse welcomes travellers and newcomers with clean beds, hot tea and quiet reading rooms.
projects.amphitheatre: The amphitheatre is a stone bowl on the hillside where the village gathers for story circle.
projects.festival-lawn: The festival lawn is a wide commons under glowing arches, made for shared feasts and round dances.
projects.water-tower: The water tower keeps the irrigation lines under steady pressure so that every field is watered.
projects.solar-field-2: The southern solar array adds more glass to the sun, so the village's lamps shine through the night.
projects.wind-array: The wind array turns the gentle ridge breeze into power, and does it so quietly that the birds are undisturbed.
projects.canal-bridge: The canal bridge is a stone footbridge that joins the plaza to the western workshops.
projects.tram-halt: The tram halt is a canopy, a bench and a timetable, waiting for the light-rail line to arrive.
